The city of Auburn appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do municipalities have the authority to prosecute violations of state statutes that they have not adopted as part of their municipal codes?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that absent explicit legislative direction municipalities may only charge violations of their municipal codes and that there has been no such legislative direction. In particular, the Court held that the Interlocal Cooperation Act (Washington Revised Code §39.34), which declares that local governments must utilize their own courts to carry out their responsibility to prosecute misdemeanor offenses committed within their jurisdictions, only addresses the fiscal responsibilities of local governments for the costs associated with prosecuting misdemeanor offenses in those courts and does not grant municipalities the authority to prosecute violations of state statutes.

title: State of Washington v. Rowland
facts: Petitioner Michael Rowland was convicted of first degree murder and taking a motor vehicle without permission in the Superior Court for Snohomish County. Based upon the judge’s finding of deliberate cruelty, Rowland was sentenced to an exceptional sentence. Rowland subsequently filed a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals challenging the calculation of his offender score. After the state of Washington conceded that Rowland’s offender score had been improperly calculated, the Washington Court of Appeals remanded the case for resentencing. On remand, the superior court imposed a standard range sentence corresponding to the reduced offender score and reimposed the sentence enhancement for deliberate cruelty. Rowland appealed his sentence, asserting that a jury finding was required to support the exceptional sentence under the United States Supreme Court’s decision in Blakely v. Washington. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Rowland’s sentence. Rowland appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the requirements of Blakely v. Washington regarding the need to submit aggravating sentencing factors to the jury apply to Rowland’s resentencing?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as the superior court did not disturb the original findings of fact supporting Rowland’s exceptional sentence and did not increase the sentence on remand, no jury finding was required.

title: State of Washington v. Lyons
facts: A Yakima District Court judge issued a warrant to search petitioner Patrick Lyons’ property on the basis of an affidavit provided by the Yakima Police Department which detailed information provided by a confidential source indicating that there was a marijuana growing operation on Lyons’ property. After the subsequent search revealed marijuana plants, supplies for packaging marijuana, and a large quantity of mushrooms, Lyons was charged with manufacturing marijuana, possesion of marijuana with intent to deliver, and possession of mushrooms with intent to deliver. Lyons moved to suppress the evidence derived from the search on grounds that because the affidavit said nothing about the timing of the confidential source’s observation, it failed to state timely probable cause. The trial court granted Lyons’ motion. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that language in the affidavit stating that the confidential source contacted the Yakima Police Department “within the last 48 hours” could be read to apply both to the time of contact and to the time of the confidential source’s observations. Lyons appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the affidavit submitted to the Yakima District Court establish timely probable cause?
conclusions: Justice Wiggins’ opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that because the Yakima District Court needed to be able to decide whether the passage of time was so prolonged that it was no longer probable that a search would reveal criminal activity or evidence, it needed to be provided with more specific information regarding the date of the confidential source’s observations. Thus, the Court held that the affidavit did not provide sufficient support for the Yakima District Court’s finding of timely probable cause.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition
